Title: Circular economy applications in railway infrastructure: A comprehensive evidence-based review

Abstract: Circular economy (CE) has emerged as a widely-recognized and vital paradigm across multiple sectors of the construction industry. Considering the complexity of ballasted and ballastless railway tracks, CE has remarkable potential to be employed throughout their whole lifecycle towards sustainability. This review paper examines the implementation of CE based on 10R principles—refute, rethink, reduce, reuse, repair, refurbish, remanufacture, repurpose, recycle, and recover—on all components of substructure and superstructure of ballasted and ballastless railway tracks, covering the potential applications from design and construction to maintenance and end-of-life stages. In this context, promotion of CE in railway infrastructure can be achieved not only by enhancing the use of recycled materials and byproducts during the construction and maintenance stages, but also by leveraging digital information technologies. Tools such as material passport, 3D printing, and virtual reality, will further facilitate the implementation of CE principles from the earlier stages of the design lifecycle. Moreover, the state-of-the-art inspection technologies based on the remote sensing and Internet of things (IoT) can be employed to extend the lifespan of track components and apply optimized preventive maintenance activities based on as-needed repairs. In this context, digital platforms like geographical information system (GIS), building information model (BIM), and digital twin, enable the employment of these advanced technologies for promotion of CE based on 10R principles. The characterized strategies will pave the route to Net Zero by 2050 by involvement in the reduction of material quantities from design and construction efficiencies towards changing inspection and maintenance activities, highlighting reduction of CO2 intensity. © 2025 The Author(s)

Title: Digital technologies in circular construction: a structured mapping of technology, strategy and lifecycle integration
Source title: Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering
Affiliations: Human–Environment–Technology (HET) Systems Centre, Mykolas Romeris University, Ateities g. 20, Vilnius, LT-08303, Lithuania
Authors with affiliations: Waqar A., Human–Environment–Technology (HET) Systems Centre, Mykolas Romeris University, Ateities g. 20, Vilnius, LT-08303, Lithuania
Abstract: The transition toward a Circular Economy (CE) in the construction sector increasingly relies on advanced digital technologies that enhance resource efficiency, material traceability, and lifecycle optimisation. This systematic review applies Screening Papers Algorithm (SPA) integrated with a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) workflow to identify 112 high-quality peer-reviewed studies published between 2016 and 2025. Scientometric mapping demonstrates steady growth in scientific output, broader international collaboration, and a thematic evolution from general sustainability discussions toward highly data-driven circularity applications. Digital technologies including Building Information Modelling (BIM), the Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Smart Data Analytics, Digital Twin (DT) systems, Blockchain (BC), Robotics and Automation (R&A), Computer Vision (CV), Radio-Frequency Identification (RFID), Three-Dimensional Printing Systems (3PS), Digital Project Management (DPM), and Material Passport Platforms (MPP) were classified and mapped against seven Circular Economy strategies and four value-chain phases. The findings reveal strong digital maturity in Sustainable Planning, Material Flow optimisation, and Lifecycle Design, driven predominantly by Building Information Modelling, Internet of Things sensors, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning analytics, and Digital Twin platforms. In contrast, the Reuse and Recycling phase and Resource and Safety Frameworks exhibit limited digital integration, especially in end-of-life activities such as deconstruction, material recovery, and circular reintegration. Cross-technology synergy analysis indicates well-developed linkages such as Building Information Modelling–Internet of Things and Building Information Modelling–Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning, while combinations such as Blockchain–Material Passport Platforms and Robotics–Computer Vision remain nascent. This review proposes a multi-layered Digital Circular Construction Framework that demonstrates how interconnected digital ecosystems operationalise circularity across the built environment and identifies critical research gaps requiring advancement, particularly in authenticated material traceability, automated deconstruction processes, and circular value-chain intelligence. © The Author(s) under exclusive licence to International Center for Numerical Methods in Engineering (CIMNE) 2026.

Title: Method Development for the Quantification of Urban Mining Potentials at District Level
Authors with affiliations: Ettl L.A., Technische Universität München, München, Germany; Ehlers N., Technische Universität München, München, Germany; Lang W., Technische Universität München, München, Germany
Abstract: This study addresses determining quantity and material composition for a specific district using CityGML data. The methodology integrates multiple databases, enabling the calculation of the timeframe within which the identified building materials will be converted back into construction waste based on certain assumptions, such as renovation or demolition. With knowledge of the material composition and quantity, targeted urban mining measures can be implemented. Recycled construction waste can be used to produce new construction materials for the industry. Additionally, this research assesses whether the material cycle within the neighbourhood can be closed by reusing the recovered building materials. During the investigation of a specific district in Germany, significant potential was identified, particularly for the building material groups concrete and steel. The generated data also facilitates the estimation of “grey emissions” released during the production of the building materials present in the neighbourhood. Beyond critically examining the potential of urban mining, the results also provide specific recommendations for stakeholders along the construction value chain. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2025.

Abstract: Digital technologies are considered enablers of circular economy implementation in the built environment. Literature mainly focuses on conceptual or review studies examining the role of digital tools (e.g., material passport and building information modelling) to close the material loops. There is a lack of understanding of how digital technologies are implemented in real-life and whether they offer value to the industry actors. This study conducted a multiple-case study to collect empirical evidence from Dutch social housing organizations actively applying circular principles in new construction, renovation, maintenance, and demolition projects. Our findings suggest that artificial intelligence, digital twins, and scanning technologies support data collection, integration, and analysis for slowing the loops strategies (i.e., maintenance), while digital marketplaces facilitate material reuse, enabling narrowing and closing the loops. This study identified 12 challenges that hinder the broader adoption of digital technologies that are associated with the technological, cultural, market, and regulatory factors. © 2022

Title: Regenerative twins as catalysts for circular, net-zero readiness in built environments: A systematic review of enablers, applications and challenges
Affiliations: University of Salford, United Kingdom; Global Banking School, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Mbabu A., University of Salford, United Kingdom; Amaechi C.V., Global Banking School, United Kingdom; Underwood J., University of Salford, United Kingdom
Abstract: The construction sector contributes 34% of global energy-related CO2 emissions and approximately 50% of global material extraction, yet material circularity has declined from 9.1% in 2018 to 6.9% in 2025. This review examines regenerative digital twins, defined as digital twins that encode material flow, embodied carbon, and end-of-life reuse potential, as enabling infrastructure for circular, net-zero-ready built environments. A PRISMA 2020 systematic review of Scopus and Google Scholar (2015 to 2026) yielded 88 studies after deduplication and two-stage screening, synthesised using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis. Publication growth is exponential, with a relative growth rate of 0.41 per year and a doubling time of 1.69 years. Enabler concentration is moderate (Herfindahl-Hirschman Index of 0.179), with application technologies dominant. A Jaccard Index (JI) of 0.455 indicates moderate integration between the regenerative-twin and broader circularity literatures. Enablers cluster into perception, network, storage, application, and design-process categories. Applications concentrate in the design and operational stages, and end-of-life regenerative feedback loops represent a critical research void, covering only 9% of studies. Challenges divide into technical barriers such as interoperability and standardisation, and socio-economic obstacles such as absent secondary-material markets, regulatory lag, and trust deficits. Policymakers should mandate standardised material passport schemas and incentivise secondary-material markets, while practitioners require interoperable BIM, LCA, and digital twin platforms and upskilling in circular design. The review distinguishes regenerative twins from generic digital twins, introduces four bibliometric indicators of field maturity, exposes the end-of-life research void, and proposes a testable framework linking enablers, applications, and challenges. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Integrating Digital Twins and Material Passports for Circular Built Environment Management
Affiliations: School of Engineering, Design and Built Environment, Western Sydney University, Parramatta City Campus, Sydney, 2150, NSW, Australia; RMIT University, Melbourne, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Tabrizi T.B., School of Engineering, Design and Built Environment, Western Sydney University, Parramatta City Campus, Sydney, 2150, NSW, Australia; Shooshtarian S., RMIT University, Melbourne, Australia; Ghafoor S., RMIT University, Melbourne, Australia
Abstract: The built environment faces urgent pressures to transition towards circular economy practices, requiring digital innovations that can overcome persistent information gaps. This paper proposes the integration of digital twins and material passports as a practical framework for enabling circularity in building lifecycle management. Digital twins provide dynamic, data-rich representations of assets, while material passports capture detailed information on material composition, provenance, and reuse potential. Synthesised within one platform, these technologies offer a systematic approach to design, operation, renovation, and end-of-life management. Drawing on an extensive review of recent literature, industry initiatives, and pilot projects, this study develops a conceptual DT–MP framework that addresses current fragmentation in data flows and decision-making. The analysis highlights how integration can enhance resource efficiency, extend asset lifespans, and optimise recovery at end-of-life, while also identifying barriers such as data standardisation, technical complexity, and organisational resistance. The paper contributes a theoretically grounded framework supported by evidence from practice-based literature and international projects. The findings underscore the transformative potential of DT–MP integration in advancing circular economy outcomes and outline directions for research and policy to enable broader adoption. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Title: Integrated BIM-GIS framework for holistic building stock assessment using 5D geo-modeling and digital twin concepts
Affiliations: Construction and Project Management Research Institute, Housing and Building National Research Centre, Giza, Egypt; Department of Geography and GIS, Faculty of African Postgraduate Studies, Cairo University, Giza, Egypt; 3D Geoscan, Alexandria, Egypt
Authors with affiliations: Elshaboury N., Construction and Project Management Research Institute, Housing and Building National Research Centre, Giza, Egypt; AlMetwaly W.M., Department of Geography and GIS, Faculty of African Postgraduate Studies, Cairo University, Giza, Egypt; Hesham A., Construction and Project Management Research Institute, Housing and Building National Research Centre, Giza, Egypt; Abbas A., 3D Geoscan, Alexandria, Egypt
Abstract: Rapid urbanization has resulted in enormous quantities of demolition waste in recent years. Designing effective waste management strategies requires assessment of generated waste during the end-of-life stage of buildings; however, information on the quantity and composition of building stock is lacking. This paper presents a robust bottom-up approach using 5D geo-modeling and digital twin concepts to predict building stocks and analyze their spatial distribution by leveraging the capabilities of building information modeling (BIM) and geographic information system (GIS). The material intensity and composition are estimated based on on-site investigations, laser scanning to capture detailed building geometry, and a BIM model to represent building components digitally. Additionally, the spatial distribution of building stock is modeled based on a GIS model. The proposed approach is demonstrated and verified in a case study of 23 typical residential buildings in an Egyptian district. The proposed BIM-GIS framework is a potential game-changer in the architecture, engineering, and construction industry. It thereby promotes effective waste management strategies across various districts by assessing their building stock. © 2025 Elsevier Ltd

Title: A parametric approach to defining archetypes for an integrated material stocks and flows analysis and life cycle assessment of built stocks
Source title: Proceedings of the International Conference of Architectural Science Association
Affiliations: Université Catholique de Louvain, Louvain-la-Neuve, Belgium

Abstract: Archetyping is a method for developing representative models of groups of buildings or infrastructure assets that share similar attributes. They typically focus on buildings and often support a single assessment method, such as urban building energy modelling, regardless of other significant flows (e.g. materials). Simplifications in developing archetypes and the inability to represent the distribution of flows across scales of the built environment reduce the precision of a model, which is critical in conducting a robust assessment that yields useful results. This paper aims to present an archetyping approach that supports an integrated life cycle assessment and material flow analysis of stock assets. As such, developed archetypes represent buildings, infrastructure, vegetation and soils. Built assets are defined as nested sets of assemblies, elements and materials. To improve reliability, we couple material compositions with geometrical data through the use of geographic information systems. We present the procedure for defining archetypes, and apply it to a building and transport infrastructure asset. The high resolution of the proposed archetyping approach enables a very high data granularity. This granularity enables a more detailed modelling of different scenarios, as well as dynamic life cycle assessment, and provides a high spatial resolution. © 2022 and published by the Architectural Science Association (ANZAScA).

Abstract: Rapid population growth is increasing housing demand and accelerating the expansion of the built environment in Egypt. However, practical and sustainable residential building decarbonization remains constrained by limited supplies of supplementary cementitious materials, limited structural timber resources, code restrictions on cement reduction, and cost sensitivity. This study evaluates two Egyptian multi-unit residential case studies—one affordable housing project and one middle-class housing project—to assess whether wall-system substitution can reduce both embodied and operational carbon under local material, code, and cost constraints. An integrated BIM-based digital twin workflow was used to link quantity takeoff, finite-element structural assessment, and whole-building energy simulation. An architectural BIM model was used for material quantification, wall-system definition, and energy-model inputs. A structural model was used to assess the effects of reducing wall density on reinforcement and concrete demand under gravity and seismic load combinations. Operational performance was assessed through cooling-focused energy simulations under hot-arid climatic conditions representative of Egypt’s new desert cities. Alternative wall systems were then evaluated through scenario- based material substitution and revised structural and energy assessments. The results show that reinforcement, concrete, and wall- core materials account for about 80% of total embodied carbon, while cooling accounts for about 72% of operational emissions. Non-structural cement uses, mainly mortars and finishes, account for 36% of total cement demand, ranging from 161 to 229 tons per building across the two case studies. Replacing conventional partition walls with lightweight, energy-efficient alternatives reduced embodied carbon by up to 35.2%, operational carbon by about 15.7% to 16.5%, and total life-cycle carbon by about 17.4% to 17.5% over a 60- year service life. The average savings per building corresponded to avoiding about 30 tons of steel, 165 m3 of ready-mix concrete, and 191 m3 of mortar, with net cost savings of about 3.15 million EGP per building. These results identify a practical pathway toward more sustainable, lower-carbon Egyptian residential buildings without increasing project cost. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: Construction and demolition activities are significant contributors to waste generation worldwide. As population growth accelerates worldwide, the amount of construction and demolition waste (C&DW) will increase proportionally unless proactive measures are implemented. This study analyzes the evolving research landscape on utilizing Building Information Modeling (BIM) technologies to advance sustainable C&DW management practices. A comprehensive text-mining analysis is conducted on 493 scholarly publications covering evolutions from January 2009 to February 2024 using the PRISMA framework. The research objectives are: (i) to identify key themes in domain of BIM technology in C&DW management using VOSviewer, (ii) to map the temporal evolution of research focus using SciMAT, and (iii) to identify emerging thematic trends.Co-occurrence analysis reveals three major research themes: (i) the use of digital twins and prefabrication for waste reduction, (ii) integrating environmental impact assessments, and (iii) data-driven decision-making. Strategic diagrams produced by SciMAT software uncover shifting priorities over the study period, with “reuse and recycling” emerging as motor themes, and “Prefabrication” (CIT = 481), “Decision Making” (CIT = 66), “Material Passport” (CIT = 92), and “Digital Twin” (CIT = 44) emerging as high-centrality and transversal themes. Temporal evolution mapping unveiled progressive integration of BIM tools such as (i) digital twins (TLS = 34, OCC = 9) and (ii) prefabrication (TLS = 40, OCC = 14), presenting opportunities to optimize waste reduction. This study offers a robust overview of the field, aiming to inform a diverse audience, including researchers from various disciplines, policymakers and industry professionals interested in advancing sustainable practices in C&DW management through innovative digital solutions. © 2024 The Authors
